title: Phone number
description: Our junior developer wrote a simple phone verification program in C. It works fine for most people... until someone curious or naughty steps in. Now, it's your job to be that curious—and perhaps naughty—person, and find out how to make this program break and behave in ways the developer never intended.
As you try and complete this challenge, you can understand the various ways in which this program can cause critical problems which we don't want!
writeup: The maximum value an int can store is 2,147,483,647. As you can see, when you enter something bigger than the maximum value, we encounter something known as an "Integer Overflow" and other problems. This can be dangerous for various reasons such as a person can login into another person's account using a different number, as you can get the idea already, that the confirmation is sent to the wrong numbers.

What happens under the hood is as the following. When you enter a number more than the maximum value, remember at the end of the day all the computer understands is ones and zeroes. i.e. whether electricity is flowing or not. So when we enter something bigger, the number wraps around and flips its bits, like a car's odometer rolling from 999999 to 000000—or in binary, rolling into the sign bit which sometimes makes the number turn negative, you can check more in detail by searching about integer overflow in detail! This gives us weird numbers which we never intended to get.

If the hacker tries to enter a string or a character, scanf("%d", ...) sees the first character, realizes it isn't an integer and immediately stops reading. Which results in the variable phone staying untouched and therefore uninitialized (holding the leftover data which C got from the RAM), and the phone number becomes any garbage number.
